Low numbers are expected when the evidence is thin: about 0.3 means a guess among several plausible spots, about 0.6 means it is the most likely spot but it could easily be elsewhere, about 0.9 means you have seen it there repeatedly at this time of day and nothing has changed. After someone has left the house the robot is asked about chore things (vacuum cleaner, laundry basket, dog bowl, watering can). So what matters is where each object is WHILE IN USE and just before, at the time of day that use happens, not only where it rests between uses.

Low numbers are expected when the evidence is thin: about 0.3 means a guess among several plausible spots, about 0.6 means it is the most likely spot but it could easily be elsewhere, about 0.9 means you have seen it there repeatedly at this time of day and nothing has changed. Do not give the same number every time.

After someone has left the house the robot is asked about chore things (vacuum cleaner, laundry basket, dog bowl, watering can). So what matters is where each object is WHILE IN USE and just before, at the time of day that use happens, not only where it rests between uses.

About 10 minutes after each question the resident tells the robot where the object turned out to be; those show up in the sightings below like any other sighting.

Answer with one spot name from the list above (the object is somewhere in the house; if it is being used or carried right now, name the spot it is most likely to be at or next to).

Confidence is the probability, from 0 to 1, that the spot you name is right. Low numbers are expected when the evidence is thin: about 0.3 means a guess among several plausible spots, about 0.6 means it is the most likely spot but it could easily be elsewhere, about 0.9 means you have seen it there repeatedly at this time of day and nothing has changed. Do not give the same number every time.

After someone has left the house the robot is asked about chore things (vacuum cleaner, laundry basket, dog bowl, watering can). So what matters is where each object is WHILE IN USE and just before, at the time of day that use happens, not only where it rests between uses.

About 10 minutes after each question the resident tells the robot where the object turned out to be; those show up in the sightings below like any other sighting.

Answer with one spot name from the list above (the object is somewhere in the house; if it is being used or carried right now, name the spot it is most likely to be at or next to).

Confidence is the probability, from 0 to 1, that the spot you name is right. Low numbers are expected when the evidence is thin: about 0.3 means a guess among several plausible spots, about 0.6 means it is the most likely spot but it could easily be elsewhere, about 0.9 means you have seen it there repeatedly at this time of day and nothing has changed. Do not give the same number every time.

So what matters is where each object is WHILE IN USE and just before, at the time of day that use happens, not only where it rests between uses.

Low numbers are expected when the evidence is thin: about 0.3 means a guess among several plausible spots, about 0.6 means it is the most likely spot but it could easily be elsewhere, about 0.9 means you have seen it there repeatedly at this time of day and nothing has changed. Do not give the same number every time.

Low numbers are expected when the evidence is thin: about 0.3 means a guess among several plausible spots, about 0.6 means it is the most likely spot but it could easily be elsewhere, about 0.9 means you have seen it there repeatedly at this time of day and nothing has changed. Low numbers are expected when the evidence is thin: about 0.3 means a guess among several plausible spots, about 0.6 means it is the most likely spot but it could easily be elsewhere, about 0.9 means you have seen it there repeatedly at this time of day and nothing has changed. Do not give the same number every time.

After someone has left the house the robot is asked about chore things (vacuum cleaner, laundry basket, dog bowl, watering can). So what matters is where each object is WHILE IN USE and just before, at the time of day that use happens, not only where it rests between uses.

About 10 minutes after each question the resident tells the robot where the object turned out to be; those show up in the sightings below like any other sighting.

Confidence is the probability, from 0 to 1, that the spot you name is right. Low numbers are expected when the evidence is thin: about 0.3 means a guess among several plausible spots, about 0.6 means it is the most likely spot but it could easily be elsewhere, about 0.9 means you have seen it there repeatedly at this time of day and nothing has changed. Do not give the same number every time.

So what matters is where each object is WHILE IN USE and just before, at the time of day that use happens, not only where it rests between uses.

Confidence is the probability, from 0 to 1, that the spot you name is right. Low numbers are expected when the evidence is thin: about 0.3 means a guess among several plausible spots, about 0.6 means it is the most likely spot but it could easily be elsewhere, about 0.9 means you have seen it there repeatedly at this time of day and nothing has changed. Do not give the same number every time.

After someone has left the house the robot is asked about chore things (vacuum cleaner, laundry basket, dog bowl, watering can). So what matters is where each object is WHILE IN USE and just before, at the time of day that use happens, not only where it rests between uses.

About 10 minutes after each question the resident tells the robot where the object turned out to be; those show up in the sightings below like any other sighting.

Answer with one spot name from the list above (the object is somewhere in the house; if it is being used or carried right now, name the spot it is most likely to be at or next to).

Confidence is the probability, from 0 to 1, that the spot you name is right. Low numbers are expected when the evidence is thin: about 0.3 means a guess among several plausible spots, about 0.6 means it is the most likely spot but it could easily be elsewhere, about 0.9 means you have seen it there repeatedly at this time of day and nothing has changed. Do not give the same number every time.

So what matters is where each object is WHILE IN USE and just before, at the time of day that use happens, not only where it rests between uses.

Low numbers are expected when the evidence is thin: about 0.3 means a guess among several plausible spots, about 0.6 means it is the most likely spot but it could easily be elsewhere, about 0.9 means you have seen it there repeatedly at this time of day and nothing has changed. Do not give the same number every time.

After someone has left the house the robot is asked about chore things (vacuum cleaner, laundry basket, dog bowl, watering can). So what matters is where each object is WHILE IN USE and just before, at the time of day that use happens, not only where it rests between uses.

About 10 minutes after each question the resident tells the robot where the object turned out to be; those show up in the sightings below like any other sighting.

Answer with one spot name from the list above (the object is somewhere in the house; if it is being used or carried right now, name the spot it is most likely to be at or next to).

Confidence is the probability, from 0 to 1, that the spot you name is right. Low numbers are expected when the evidence is thin: about 0.3 means a guess among several plausible spots, about 0.6 means it is the most likely spot but it could easily be elsewhere, about 0.9 means you have seen it there repeatedly at this time of day and nothing has changed. Do not give the same number every time.

messages.content: You help a home robot keep track of where household things are. Read the robot's notes and answer with JSON only.

The robot walked through every room on day 0 at 18:00 and since then patrols every room once a day at 03:00, listing what is on every spot and who is in the room. Pockets and bags are not looked into.

Residents:
- Felix (in their early twenties) is a student. Every day: at classes from about 8:40 to 2:30, then studying at home. Hobbies: board games, cycling, calls with family, reading.
- Aisha (in their sixties) is retired. Every day: home most of the day, with a morning walk and afternoon errands. Hobbies: cycling, gaming, photography. Aisha looks after the household's dog.

Rooms and spots:
- bathroom: bathroom_shelf_ba1, medicine_cabinet_ba1, sink_ba_ba1, towel_rack_ba1
- bedroom_1: bed_b1, bedroom_floor_b1, desk_b1, dresser_b1, nightstand_b1, wardrobe_b1
- entry: entry_floor_e1, entry_hook_e1, entry_table_e1, shoe_rack_e1
- kitchen: chair_k1, counter_k1, cupboard_k1, dish_rack_k1, drawer_k_k1, floor_k_k1, kitchen_table_k1, pantry_shelf_k1, sink_k1
- living: armchair_l1, bookshelf_l1, coffee_table_l1, couch_l1, floor_l_l1, side_table_l1, tv_stand_l1
- storage: storage_floor_s1, storage_shelf_s1

WHEN THE ROBOT IS ASKED: the residents ask where something is when they are about to use it, a few minutes around the start of a meal, cooking, a work or study session, evening TV, a shower, bedtime, a hobby, and they ask about the things that activity uses (plates, glasses and bottles at meals; pans, knives and boards when cooking; laptop, mug, notebook and headphones at work; remote, blanket and snack bowl for TV; toiletries in the bathroom). messages.content: You help a home robot keep track of where household things are. Read the robot's notes and answer with JSON only.

The robot walked through every room on day 0 at 18:00 and since then patrols every room once a day at 03:00, listing what is on every spot and who is in the room. Pockets and bags are not looked into.

Residents:
- Felix (in their early twenties) is a student. Every day: at classes from about 8:40 to 2:30, then studying at home. Hobbies: board games, cycling, calls with family, reading.
- Aisha (in their sixties) is retired. Every day: home most of the day, with a morning walk and afternoon errands. Hobbies: cycling, gaming, photography. Aisha looks after the household's dog.

Rooms and spots:
- bathroom: bathroom_shelf_ba1, medicine_cabinet_ba1, sink_ba_ba1, towel_rack_ba1
- bedroom_1: bed_b1, bedroom_floor_b1, desk_b1, dresser_b1, nightstand_b1, wardrobe_b1
- entry: entry_floor_e1, entry_hook_e1, entry_table_e1, shoe_rack_e1
- kitchen: chair_k1, counter_k1, cupboard_k1, dish_rack_k1, drawer_k_k1, floor_k_k1, kitchen_table_k1, pantry_shelf_k1, sink_k1
- living: armchair_l1, bookshelf_l1, coffee_table_l1, couch_l1, floor_l_l1, side_table_l1, tv_stand_l1
- storage: storage_floor_s1, storage_shelf_s1

WHEN THE ROBOT IS ASKED: the residents ask where something is when they are about to use it, a few minutes around the start of a meal, cooking, a work or study session, evening TV, a shower, bedtime, a hobby, and they ask about the things that activity uses (plates, glasses and bottles at meals; pans, knives and boards when cooking; laptop, mug, notebook and headphones at work; remote, blanket and snack bowl for TV; toiletries in the bathroom). After someone has left the house the robot is asked about chore things (vacuum cleaner, laundry basket, dog bowl, watering can). So what matters is where each object is WHILE IN USE and just before, at the time of day that use happens, not only where it rests between uses.

About 10 minutes after each question the resident tells the robot where the object turned out to be; those show up in the sightings below like any other sighting.

Answer with one spot name from the list above (the object is somewhere in the house; if it is being used or carried right now, name the spot it is most likely to be at or next to).

Confidence is the probability, from 0 to 1, that the spot you name is right. Low numbers are expected when the evidence is thin: about 0.3 means a guess among several plausible spots, about 0.6 means it is the most likely spot but it could easily be elsewhere, about 0.9 means you have seen it there repeatedly at this time of day and nothing has changed.
